Q — Can there be a universal conception of human rights? Examine the debate between universalism and cultural relativism. (UPSC 2021)
Human rights (born after WWII, UDHR 1948) claim to be universal — held by all humans just because they are human.
They rest on Locke’s natural rights and Kant’s human dignity; their central claim is ‘universalism’.
Cultural relativists (Asian values, communitarians) say ‘universal’ rights are really Western values — a form of cultural imperialism.

Q — What do you understand by the three generations of human rights? (UPSC 2018)
The Czech jurist Karel Vasak (1979) classified human rights into three ‘generations’, echoing the French Revolution’s liberty-equality-fraternity.
1st generation = civil & political (‘blue’) rights — negative, restrain the state (life, liberty, vote).
2nd generation = socio-economic & cultural (‘red’) rights — positive, require state action (work, education).
3rd generation = solidarity (‘green’) rights — collective (self-determination, peace, development, environment).
The ‘three generations’ framework was proposed in
at Strasbourg, classifying human rights along the lines of the French Revolution’s ‘liberty, equality, fraternity’.
First generation — civil and political rights

rights that restrain the state — life, liberty, property, equality before law, freedom of expression and the vote. They belong to the liberal tradition and were recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
Second generation — socio-economic and cultural rights

rights requiring state action — the right to work, education, equal wages and social security. Championed by socialist states, they were recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Both first and second generations are
rights ‘exercised in solidarity’ — self-determination, peace, development, a healthy environment and humanitarian assistance — responding to global, developmental and ecological concerns.

The generations map the historical widening of rights from the individual against the state (civil-political), to the individual’s welfare through the state (socio-economic), to humanity’s shared claims (solidarity) — though critics note that treating them as a sequence can wrongly imply the later ones are less urgent than the first.
Q — Critically examine the ‘Asian values’ critique of human rights and the challenges to their implementation. (UPSC 2016)
‘Asian values’ (Lee Kuan Yew, 1990s) argue human rights are Western and not truly universal.
Rooted in Confucianism, they put the community/family and duties above the individual, and rank socio-economic rights above political ones.
They claim national self-determination bars outside interference in a state’s human-rights record.
Implementation is hard because rights are anti-state yet states are their only guardians — so enforcement means ‘changing the conduct of states’.

(UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 5) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the meaning, nature and theories of rights (natural, legal, moral, conservative/historical, social-welfare, Marxist, and contemporary — libertarian, communitarian, multicultural); types of rights and the negative/positive distinction; the doctrine of ‘rights as trumps’; and human rights — the three generations, the ‘Asian values’ critique, and the universalism vs cultural-relativism debate. Must-know thinkers:  Laski, Locke, Paine, Bentham, Burke, T.H. Green, Kant, Dworkin, Joseph Raz, Nozick, Walzer, Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh, Karel Vasak, Lee Kuan Yew, Isaiah Berlin, Susan Moller Okin, Amartya Sen. PYQ trend:  universal conception of human rights (2021), right to property (2020), rights as trumps (2019), three generations (2018), implementation/changing conduct of states (2016), natural rights (2015). Master Questions Q — Critically examine the theories of rights — natural, legal, moral, conservative/historical, social-welfare and Marxist. ‘Idea of natural rights.’ Comment. (UPSC 2015) Gist — the spine to recall A ‘right’ is a condition of social life we need to be our best self (Laski) — and thinkers disagree on where rights come from. Natural (Locke): rights come from nature, before the state; Legal (Bentham): only the state creates rights — natural rights are ‘nonsense on stilts’. Moral (Kant, Green): rights flow from reason/morality; Conservative (Burke): rights grow from custom and history. Marxist: rights are a ‘bourgeois’ tool of the ruling class; social-welfare theory ties rights to the good of society. Model Answer For  Laski , “rights are those conditions of social life without which no man can seek, in general, to be himself at his best.” A right is a modern, originally  anti-statist  concept that limits the power of state and society; the theories differ chiefly on the  source  of rights. Natural rights  (17th–18th c.): rights are a corollary of  natural law , inherent in human nature and not granted by the state — the ‘self-evident truths’ of the American (1776) and French declarations.  Locke  (life, liberty, property) is its champion;  Tom Paine  gives it a teleological basis. Legal rights  ( Bentham ): the  state  is the real source — ‘real laws give birth to real rights’; natural rights are “nonsense upon stilts” and ‘anarchical fallacies’.  Salmond : a legal right is ‘an interest protected and recognised by the rule of law’. Moral rights  ( Kant, T.H. Green ): rights flow from the dictates of reason and moral personality, treating persons ‘as ends, not means’.  Conservative/historical  ( Burke ): rights are the product of a long historical process and  custom , not abstract nature — he condemned the French Revolution’s ‘metaphysical abstractions’; critics reply that custom also sanctioned sati and untouchability. Social-welfare & Marxist.  The  social-welfare  theory (Bentham’s utilitarian legacy, Roscoe Pound) ties rights to the ‘greatest happiness’, criticised as too vague. The  Marxist  view calls rights a ‘bourgeois concept’ — ‘class law’ in the superstructure giving the common man no substantive gain in a class-divided society. Conclusion.  Laski’s  social-democratic synthesis best reconciles them: ‘every state is known by the rights it maintains’, and rights, though rooted in social good, must secure both individual liberty and social justice — uniting the moral force of natural rights with the enforceability of legal rights. Q — Discuss the doctrine of ‘rights as trumps’ (Dworkin) and its critics. Can the right to privacy trump state interest? (UPSC 2019) Gist — the spine to recall Dworkin says individual rights are ‘trumps’ — they beat ordinary policy goals, even the community’s interest. So the government cannot override a genuine right just because doing so is useful for the majority. There is no simple trade-off: e.g., privacy cannot normally be sacrificed to ‘national security’. But even Dworkin allows narrow exceptions (when only a weak form of the right is at stake, or the cost is huge); Raz and utilitarians disagree. Model Answer In  Taking Rights Seriously ,  Ronald Dworkin  argues that individual rights are  ‘trumps’  — they take precedence over collective goals, even the interest of the community or state. Rights are not what the state chooses to grant; ‘the sole purpose of the state is the maintenance of rights’. He attacks the  positivist and utilitarian  view that a person is entitled only to state-given rights. On the trumps model there is  no easy trade-off  between a right and a policy benefit: a genuine right cannot be overridden merely because doing so maximises welfare. Right to privacy.  It follows that a right such as  privacy  cannot ordinarily be ‘trumped’ by an appeal to national security — the right sets a limit that policy must respect. This is why the doctrine underpins strong judicial protection of fundamental rights (in India, privacy has been read as intrinsic to the right to life). Dworkin’s own exceptions.  Rights may be compromised in two narrow cases: (i) when the value the right protects is at stake only in some  attenuated form ; and (ii) when the  cost  of honouring the right far exceeds its benefit.  Habermas  similarly argues that even human dignity, though it usually prevails, may be ‘partially defeated’ in unavoidable circumstances. Critics.  Utilitarians reject the priority of rights over aggregate welfare, and  Joseph Raz  (in  The Authority of Law ) holds that law is ‘autonomous’, with no necessary continuity between rights and morality. Conclusion.  ‘Rights as trumps’ powerfully defends the individual against majoritarian and state overreach; its qualified exceptions show that even Dworkin treats rights as near-absolute rather than wholly absolute — a via media between rigid absolutism and utilitarian expediency. Q — Can there be a universal conception of human rights? Examine the debate between universalism and cultural relativism. (UPSC 2021) Gist — the spine to recall Human rights (born after WWII, UDHR 1948) claim to be universal — held by all humans just because they are human. They rest on Locke’s natural rights and Kant’s human dignity; their central claim is ‘universalism’. Cultural relativists (Asian values, communitarians) say ‘universal’ rights are really Western values — a form of cultural imperialism. Answer: keep a universal basic minimum, but let it grow through ‘dialogue among civilisations’ rather than imposition. Model Answer Human rights emerged after the Second World War (in reaction to the Nazi atrocities), codified in the  International Bill of Rights  — the  UDHR (1948)  and the two 1966 Covenants. They rest on  Locke’s  natural rights (‘self-evident truths’) and  Kant’s  concept of  human dignity , and their defining — and most contested — claim is  universalism : basic rights belong to all ‘just because they are human’. The case for universality.  A common humanity and human dignity give everyone an equal, inalienable, permanent claim; human rights have abolished manifestly inhuman practices — sati (Raja Ram Mohan Roy as a precursor), female foeticide, genital mutilation — and now expand into new domains (the UN’s recognition of a human right to water). The relativist challenge.  Cultural relativists  (concept from  Franz Boas ) and  communitarians  argue that every culture is rational and there is no hierarchy of cultures; the ‘situated self’ is shaped by community, so ‘universal’ rights are really  Western values  — ‘cultural imperialism’. The  Asian values  school (Lee Kuan Yew, the 1993 Bangkok Declaration) stresses regional, historical and religious particularity. Value pluralism.  Isaiah Berlin  adds that values are  plural and incommensurable  — there is ‘no objective criterion’ to rank them — so the West should not impose its scheme. Yet he retains some ‘generic values’ and prizes  toleration  (Voltaire: ‘I detest what you say, yet will defend your right to say it’). Conclusion.  A universal conception is defensible only as a  basic minimum  of human dignity that is refined through  Parekh’s  ‘dialogue among civilisations’ rather than imposed ‘at gunpoint’ — universal in its core, plural in its expression. Q — What do you understand by the three generations of human rights? (UPSC 2018) Gist — the spine to recall The Czech jurist Karel Vasak (1979) classified human rights into three ‘generations’, echoing the French Revolution’s liberty-equality-fraternity. 1st generation = civil & political (‘blue’) rights — negative, restrain the state (life, liberty, vote). 2nd generation = socio-economic & cultural (‘red’) rights — positive, require state action (work, education). 3rd generation = solidarity (‘green’) rights — collective (self-determination, peace, development, environment). Model Answer The ‘three generations’ framework was proposed in  1979  by the Czech jurist  Karel Vasak  at Strasbourg, classifying human rights along the lines of the French Revolution’s ‘liberty, equality, fraternity’. First generation — civil and political rights  (the ‘blue rights’): these are  negative  rights that restrain the state — life, liberty, property, equality before law, freedom of expression and the vote. They belong to the liberal tradition and were recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Second generation — socio-economic and cultural rights  (the ‘red rights’): these are  positive  rights requiring state action — the right to work, education, equal wages and social security. Championed by socialist states, they were recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Both first and second generations are  individual-centred . Third generation — solidarity rights  (the ‘green rights’): these are  collective  rights ‘exercised in solidarity’ — self-determination, peace, development, a healthy environment and humanitarian assistance — responding to global, developmental and ecological concerns. Conclusion.  The generations map the historical widening of rights from the individual against the state (civil-political), to the individual’s welfare through the state (socio-economic), to humanity’s shared claims (solidarity) — though critics note that treating them as a sequence can wrongly imply the later ones are less urgent than the first. Q — Critically examine the ‘Asian values’ critique of human rights and the challenges to their implementation. (UPSC 2016) Gist — the spine to recall ‘Asian values’ (Lee Kuan Yew, 1990s) argue human rights are Western and not truly universal. Rooted in Confucianism, they put the community/family and duties above the individual, and rank socio-economic rights above political ones. They claim national self-determination bars outside interference in a state’s human-rights record. Implementation is hard because rights are anti-state yet states are their only guardians — so enforcement means ‘changing the conduct of states’. Model Answer The ‘Asian values’ critique arose in the 1990s, after the fall of the USSR and the rise of East Asia. Its proponents —  Lee Kuan Yew  and  Mahathir Mohamad  — trace it to  Confucianism , which prizes group harmony and duties to society over individual claims. Four claims.  (1) human rights are  not universal  and cannot be globalised; (2) Asian societies are centred on the  family/community , not the individual; (3)  socio-economic rights  rank above political rights; and (4)  national self-determination  includes domestic jurisdiction over human rights, so ‘other nations should not interfere’. The  1993 Bangkok Declaration  gave this diplomatic form, stressing ‘national and regional peculiarities’. Post-colonial and cultural-relativist thinkers reinforce it, seeing universal human rights as  cultural imperialism ; the West, in turn, dismisses Asian values as ‘soft authoritarianism’ masking the denial of political freedom. Challenges to implementation.  Human rights are inherently  anti-state , yet states are their principal guardians — so states give ‘moral guarantees’ but often fail in practice. Enforcement therefore becomes ‘a matter of  changing the conduct of states ’, which sovereignty and the non-interference claim resist.  Amartya Sen  rebuts the school: Asia’s vast diversity means there is no single ‘Asian value’, and freedom is not un-Asian. Conclusion.  The Asian-values critique rightly warns against ethnocentric imposition, but hardens into a shield for authoritarian denial of rights. The way forward is a negotiated basic minimum, monitored internationally yet advanced through dialogue rather than coercion. Q — Discuss multiculturalism and minority rights, with special reference to Kymlicka and Bhikhu Parekh. Gist — the spine to recall Multiculturalism defends the rights of minority cultures — not just to exist, but to be actively accommodated. It grew from the liberal–communitarian debate: identity is bound up with culture, so equal treatment sometimes needs special rights. Kymlicka (liberal): give ‘national minorities’ group-differentiated rights — polyethnic, special-representation and self-government rights. Parekh (post-colonial): universal principles must emerge through ‘dialogue among civilisations’, anchored in human dignity. Model Answer Multiculturalism emerged from the liberal–communitarian debate to defend the rights of  minority cultures . Since culture is part of identity, treating people as equals may require not identical but  group-specific  rights that accommodate difference. Will Kymlicka  (in  Multicultural Citizenship ) offers a  liberal  theory: liberalism itself requires protecting minority cultures because a secure cultural context is a precondition of individual autonomy. Being born into a minority culture is ‘bad brute luck’ deserving rectification — his ‘luck egalitarianism’. He grants three  group-differentiated rights : (1)  polyethnic  rights (religious/cultural practice); (2)  special representation  rights (e.g. reservation); and (3)  self-government  rights (e.g. India’s Fifth and Sixth Schedules) — but reserved for ‘national minorities’, not voluntary immigrants. Bhikhu Parekh  (in  Rethinking Multiculturalism ) takes a  post-colonial  view: multiculturalism is the ‘creative interplay’ of cultural embeddedness and plurality. He finds no logic in denying special rights to non-citizen minorities, applies a ‘harm principle’ to cultural practices, and insists universal principles must be built through  dialogue among civilisations , anchored in the shared value of  human dignity . Critiques.  Feminists ( Susan Moller Okin , ‘multiculturalism is bad for women’) warn that protecting cultures can shield patriarchy; liberals ( Amartya Sen, Brian Barry ) fear ‘ghettoisation’ and weakened national unity. Conclusion.  Multiculturalism corrects the blindness of abstract equal treatment, but must be bounded by a basic minimum of human rights — accommodating cultural difference without entrenching internal injustice. Q — Assess the significance of the right to property in political theory. (UPSC 2020) Gist — the spine to recall Property has been one of the most contested rights — seen by some as the basis of freedom, by others as the root of inequality. Liberals (Locke, Smith, Bentham): property is a natural right and the foundation of social progress. Marxists: private property is the source of class division, exploitation and alienation (Proudhon: ‘property is theft’). Middle path (Laski, Hobhouse): property has a social origin and must serve the common good — hence it was diluted from a fundamental right in India. Model Answer Few rights have been as contested as the right to property, precisely because it sits at the crossroads of  liberty and equality . The classical debate.  Plato  saw property as a source of corruption (hence communism of the guardians), while  Aristotle  linked it to virtue and rational responsibility.  Machiavelli  observed that ‘men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’. Liberal defence.  Locke  made property a  natural right  (mixing one’s labour with nature), the core of ‘possessive individualism’;  Adam Smith  and  Bentham  treated private property as essential to social progress and incentive. Socialist critique.  For  Marxists , private property is the very  basis of class division , exploitation and alienation — they distinguish personal from private (productive) property;  Proudhon  declared ‘property is theft’. The social-liberal balance.  Laski  (in  A Grammar of Politics ) treats property as an instrument of the  common good  — ‘a man of property has a stake in the country’ — and  Hobhouse  stresses its  social origin ;  Sen  and  Dworkin  tie its allocation to justice, and the Gandhian idea of  trusteeship  makes the owner a custodian for society. Conclusion.  The significance of the right to property lies in this unresolved tension: indispensable to individual freedom yet dangerous to equality — which is why the modern welfare state (and India, by demoting it from a fundamental to a legal right) treats it not as absolute but as socially conditioned. Dworkin ,  Taking Rights Seriously : ‘rights are trumps’ — override collective goals; narrow exceptions only. Negative vs positive rights:  state must NOT enter (negative) vs state MUST act (positive); welfare state combines both. Marxist:  rights = ‘bourgeois concept’ / class law in the superstructure. Human rights:  UDHR 1948 + two 1966 Covenants; based on Locke (natural rights) + Kant (human dignity); core claim = universalism. Karel Vasak  (1979): 3 generations — 1st civil-political (blue), 2nd socio-economic (red), 3rd solidarity (green). Asian values  (Lee Kuan Yew, 1993 Bangkok Declaration): community over individual; socio-economic over political; non-interference. Kymlicka : 3 group-differentiated rights (polyethnic / representation / self-government) for national minorities. Parekh : multiculturalism = ‘creative interplay’; universal principles via dialogue among civilisations. Susan Moller Okin : ‘multiculturalism is bad for women’;  Isaiah Berlin : value pluralism (incommensurable values). Right to property:  Locke/Smith  (natural, progress) vs  Marx/Proudhon  (‘property is theft’) vs  Laski/Hobhouse  (social origin, common good).
